segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: About that time King Herod laid hands on some who belonged to the assembly, to do them harm.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He had James, the brother of John, killed with the sword.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Seeing that this pleased the Jews, he went on to arrest Peter as well. This was during the days of Unleavened Bread.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: After seizing him, he put him in prison and handed him over to four squads of four soldiers to guard him, intending to bring him out before the people after the Passover.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So Peter was kept in the prison, but prayer for him was being earnestly made to God by the assembly.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When Herod was about to bring him out, that very night Peter was sleeping between two soldiers, bound with two chains, while guards in front of the door kept watch over the prison.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Suddenly an angel of the Lord stood there, and a light shone in the cell. He struck Peter on the side and woke him, saying,

segments.speaker: angel
segments.text: “Get up quickly!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And the chains fell from his hands.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The angel said to him,

segments.speaker: angel
segments.text: “Fasten your belt and put on your sandals.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He did so. Then the angel said to him,

segments.speaker: angel
segments.text: “Wrap your cloak around you and follow me.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He went out and followed, not knowing that what was happening through the angel was real; he thought he was seeing a vision.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They passed the first guard post and the second and came to the iron gate that leads into the city, which opened for them by itself. They went out and walked the length of one street, and at once the angel left him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then Peter came to himself and said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Now I truly know that the Lord sent his angel and rescued me from Herod’s hand and from everything the people of the Jews were expecting.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When he had taken this in, he went to the house of Mary, the mother of John who was also called Mark, where a good number had gathered and were praying.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When he knocked at the door of the gateway, a slave girl named Rhoda came to answer.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Recognizing Peter’s voice, in her joy she did not open the gateway but ran in and told them that Peter was standing at the gateway.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They said to her,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “You are out of your mind!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But she kept insisting that it was so. They said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “It is his angel.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But Peter kept on knocking, and when they opened they saw him and were astounded.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Motioning to them with his hand to be quiet, he described to them how the Lord had brought him out of the prison. And he said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Tell this to James and the brothers and sisters.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then he went out and travelled to another place.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When day came, there was no small commotion among the soldiers over what had become of Peter.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Herod searched for him and did not find him; he interrogated the guards and ordered them led away to execution. Then he went down from Judea to Caesarea and stayed there.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now Herod was furious with the people of Tyre and Sidon. They came to him together, and after winning over Blastus, the king’s chamberlain, they asked for peace, because their country drew its food from the king’s.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: On an appointed day Herod put on royal robes, took his seat on the platform, and began delivering a public address to them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The crowd kept shouting,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “The voice of a god, not of a human being!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Immediately an angel of the Lord struck him, because he did not give the glory to God, and he was eaten by worms and breathed his last.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But the word of God grew and multiplied.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Barnabas and Saul returned, having completed their service in Jerusalem, and they took along with them John, who was called Mark.

notes.note: The Greek word was the ordinary term for a civic gathering and the Septuagint's word for Israel assembled before God. 'Church' is the near-universal rendering and readers know what it refers to, but it now suggests a building or an institution, which the word did not. 'Assembly' is used throughout this translation so that the one Greek word appears as one English word.

This is Herod Agrippa I, grandson of Herod the Great, who ruled Judea as king from AD 41 to 44. He is a different man from the Herod of Jesus's birth and from Herod Antipas, who appears in the accounts of Jesus's trial.

Passover was followed immediately by the seven days of Unleavened Bread, and by this period either name could be used for the whole festival. 'After the Passover' here means after the festival week mentioned in verse 3 had ended. The King James Version's 'Easter' in this verse is an anachronism.
The night was divided into four watches, so four squads allowed a fresh team of four for each watch. Verse 6 shows the arrangement: two soldiers chained to the prisoner and two on guard at the door.

In the Greek of this period the word normally meant a female slave, and that is how a first-century reader would have taken it. Most English versions soften it to 'servant girl' or 'maid', which suggests a hired employee. Rhoda was most likely a slave of Mary's household, and evidently one of the believers.

The speakers seem to assume that a person has an angel who watches over them and may look or sound like them; a similar idea lies behind Matthew 18:10. Some interpreters think they mean that Peter has been killed and this is his spirit, but the word used is the normal one for an angel.

This is not James the brother of John, whose death was reported in verse 2. It is James the brother of Jesus, who by this time was a leading figure in the Jerusalem community (see Acts 15 and Galatians 1:19).

The Greek masculine plural was the ordinary way of referring to a mixed group of siblings, and here it means the members of the community, women included. Traditional versions have 'the brothers' or 'the brethren'. A minority of interpreters think a narrower group of leaders is meant.

The Greek says only that he ordered them 'led away'. The verb was a common legal term for taking someone off to punishment, especially execution, and most translators understand it so here; a guard who lost a prisoner could be made to bear the prisoner's penalty. It could mean simply that they were taken into custody.

The Greek word denotes a raised platform from which an official addressed the public or heard legal cases. It is not the word for a royal throne. Many versions have 'throne' here; others have 'tribunal', 'rostrum' or 'judgment seat'.

The Jewish historian Josephus gives an independent account of Agrippa's death in AD 44 (Antiquities, book 19). At a festival in Caesarea, the crowd hailed him as a god while he wore a dazzling robe; he did not rebuke them, was seized with violent abdominal pain, and died some days later. The verb 'struck' is the same one used of the angel waking Peter in verse 7: one blow rescues, the other destroys.

notes.phrase: having completed their service in Jerusalem
notes.note: The earliest manuscripts read 'to Jerusalem', which is difficult because Barnabas and Saul were already there (11:30) and next appear in Antioch (13:1). Other manuscripts read 'from Jerusalem', probably a correction, and many English versions follow them. The edition translated here keeps 'to Jerusalem' and punctuates so that the phrase goes with 'their service' rather than with 'returned'; this translation follows it. The service is the famine relief of 11:29–30.

candidates.reason: The plural for the believing community occurs hundreds of times, and translators divide between 'brothers', 'brothers and sisters' and 'believers', so one policy is needed.
The word recurs in the Gospels, Acts, Romans 14:10 and 2 Corinthians 5:10 as 'throne', 'tribunal' and 'judgment seat'; readers should be able to see it is one word.
It is rendered variously as 'ministry', 'service', 'mission' and 'relief' across Acts and the letters, and 'ministry' now carries clerical overtones.
It recurs in the Gospels, Acts 16:16 and Galatians 4, where 'servant girl', 'maid' and 'slave woman' obscure that one status is meant.
It is a characteristic word in Acts, rendered variously as 'with one accord', 'together' and 'unanimously'; a consistent choice would preserve Luke's refrain.
